source_spans.locator: Nature 415, published p.429, Abstract: minimum-variance combination principle, measurement of unimodal variances, model construction, and comparison with human judgments
Nature 415, equations (1)-(3): modality-specific noisy estimators, independent-Gaussian and uniform-prior assumptions, reciprocal-variance weights, and lower variance of the joint estimate
Nature 415, Figure 3a and equations (4)-(5): unimodal discrimination thresholds across four visual-noise levels and predicted visual/haptic weights
Nature 415, Figure 3b-d and equations (6)-(7): observed PSEs, PSE-derived weights, and bimodal discrimination thresholds compared with predictions

Nature 415, discussion following Figure 3: trial-randomized visual noise, weight setting within the 1-s presentation, tested discrepancies no greater than 11%, and possible discounting at larger discrepancies
Nature 415, Methods (Stimuli; Procedure): visual-depth-noise manipulation, 1-s presentations, two-interval forced-choice procedure, and four-observer characteristics

conditions: two modality-specific estimates of the same ridge height are available with measurable, condition-dependent uncertainty
the model prediction assumes independent Gaussian estimator noise and a uniform prior
derivation of an empirical modality weight from the point of subjective equality assumes the two unimodal estimators are unbiased on average
tested cross-modal height discrepancies were no greater than 11%, a regime in which both inputs affected judgments
population: four observers aged 22-33, naive to the experimental purpose, right-handed, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision
task: two-interval forced-choice comparison of raised-ridge height from visual-only, haptic-only, or simultaneous visual and haptic information
temporal_scope: each stimulus presentation lasted 1 s; visual-noise level varied randomly across trials, so condition-dependent weighting was set within the presentation interval
